leader.name: Joseph Stalin
leader.title: Chairman of the Council of Ministers

gdp_nominal.note: Western estimates put Soviet output at roughly a third of US output around 1949–50. Highly uncertain; will become a fogged range in Phase 3.

gdp_real.note: 1949 is the base year, so real GDP equals GDP at 1949 US prices at the start.

real_growth.note: Western estimates of Soviet growth during post-war reconstruction, 1948–50: lower than the official figures, but still rapid.

steel_output.note: Soviet official figure for 1949 crude steel output.

savings_overhang.note: Unspendable household savings after the confiscatory currency reform of December 1947 wiped out most wartime savings. Small but growing.

defence_spending.note: About 12% of GNP at US prices, following CIA-style dollar valuations. Highly uncertain.

active_personnel.note: Soviet armed forces after post-war demobilisation, about 2.9 million in 1948 by later-published figures.

nuclear_warheads.note: No Soviet weapon exists yet. The first test (RDS-1) came in August 1949.

population.note: Back-projected from the official figure of about 178.5 million on 1 January 1950.

consumer_shortage.note: Share of household demand left unmet in 1949: rationing ended in 1947, but queues and deficits were endemic.

population_growth_annual.note: Rough post-war growth rate. A placeholder until the cohort-component model replaces it.

sources.label: B. R. Mitchell, International Historical Statistics
Correlates of War, National Material Capabilities
Abram Bergson, The Real National Income of Soviet Russia since 1928 (1961)

output_gap.note: 'Taut planning': plans set targets slightly above normal capacity, so the economy ran about 1% above it.
